content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: thorough experimentation, although I am not familiar enough with this literature to evaluate the strength of the results.

Weaknesses: the model (Eq. 1) is not novel enough; and in addition has a critical typo that makes me uncertain as to what the authors intended.
content.summary_of_the_review:
I think this paper has good experimental work, but the modeling innovations are minor, and for this reason I can’t recommend publication.

The crux of the method is Eq. 1. Note that this has a typo I think - for this method to be NCE, and in generally to make sense, I think the denominator term needs to be 

\sum_{k=1}^m exp(sim(d_j, d’k))

Note that d_k is replaced by d’_k here - and it should be clarified that d’_1 … d’_m are sampled uniformly from some background distribution. I think this recreation is probably what the authors meant, but this is such a crucial part of the paper it’s an unfortunate mistake.

Even with that correction though I think the model in Eq. 1 is a quite simple combination of known techniques. 

As an additional comment, the introduction is a little hard to follow. It’s not clear why the “weak alignment” and “strong alignment” terms are being introduced.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes an approach to cross-lingual information retrieval (CLIR), which is essentially achieved by cross-lingual pretraining and finetuning from Wikipedia cross-lingual alignment targeted at CLIR. Convincing results are supplied in comparison to relevant methods in question answering, passage ranking, and sentence retrieval.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- An interesting and believable method coupled with good experiment breadth in terms of selected tasks.
- Empirical results seem to be quite strong.

Weaknesses:
- The draft writeup is not of particularly high quality, evident already in the introduction section and in the conclusion, which feature multiple typos and a narrative that is not facilitating information retention for the prospective reader, e.g. in the list of contributions in the introduction just to list one example.
- In the conclusion, it is entirely unclear what is meant by " But the previous approaches for multi-lingual pre-training were not concentrated on the cross-linguality." This is vague and needs to be clarified.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Writeup is poor, which hinders quality and clarity. As for the originality of the work, I am not fully equipped to qualify it, although I do notice that a number of relevant contributions to CLIR are not referred to in the literature, e.g. Litschko et al. (ECIR 2021), Vulic & Moens (SIGIR 2015) which featured adaptation via embeddings and is quite prominent, etc. That makes me somewhat skeptical of the placement of this work in relation to past contributions.
content.summary_of_the_review: I am not that familiar with the subfield of CLIR to align the contributions to related work. Methodologically, I see no serious flaws, nor do I see exceptional novelty nor creativity in the modelling approach, which is not necessarily a negative assessment. The results are believable. My main concern is the quality of the draft writeup, which can arguably be improved within revisions scope, and positioning in terms of related work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper focuses on cross-lingual information retrieval. It uses the Wikipedia pages in the same topic from different languages as a supervised signal to train the multilingual passage encoder LEXA. Hard-negatives for self-training and leveraging the PAQ dataset are also incorporated into LEXA. The experiments show that LEXA achieve very good performance on QA related retrieval tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- Good engineering value: combines many existing techniques (hard negatives, PAQ data) into one model. Utilizing Wikipedia links as effective supervised signals to train cross-lingual encoder.
- Good performance on many downstream tasks. Sufficient experiments.

Weaknesses:
- Very limited novelty: The only new idea in this paper is to utilize Wikipedia links in different languages as a pseudo-parallel corpus. Other methods are mostly just engineering tricks (hard negatives, PAQ data) without much novelty.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: Some part of the paper is not clear at all. For example, in section 3.4, you mentioned zero-shot setting and unsupervised setting, what's the difference between them? For zero-shot setting, it's not using any label data for the downstream tasks, then what's unsupervised one? In addition, your model uses Wikipedia links in different languages as a pseudo-parallel corpus, so I don't think it's any possible to have a real "unsupervised setting".
Quality: Latex errors in section 4.1 should be fixed.
Novelty: Very limited as I mentioned in Weaknesses 
Reproducibility: The author didn't provide the code, and the engineering tricks seem complex in this paper. I don't think it's easy to reproduce the result.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper has a very limited novelty, though it has a good engineering contribution. Also, the clarity can be further improved. I don't suggest accepting this paper to ICLR. I think it's more suitable as a workshop paper at NLP conferences.

content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
	This paper focuses on cross-lingual knowledge transfer. It shows the method on various tasks. 


Weakness:
1.	The writing and setting up of this paper are not very clear to me. The motivation does not convincing to me. 
2.	The novelty of the proposed method seems trivial. Contrastive learning, embedding alignment and etc have been widely discussed in the previous literature.  
3.	For XQR performance, it is not surprising that with the additional selected XOR finetuning examples, the performance will boost further. 
4.	The ablation of the paper is not ready. It would be better to see the parameter comparison or computing comparison between the proposed method and the existing methods. It is also not clear to me that the performance boost is from the proposed alignment components or other mentioned adjustments such as filtering and etc.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper is not ready for ICLR based on the current version.

content.title: LEXA: Language-agnostic Cross-consistency Training for Question Answering Tasks
content.TL;DR: We developed a novel pre-training method to improve cross-lingual consistency in a language model. We demonstrate the achieved ability on several question answering datasets.
content.abstract: Cross-lingual information retrieval (CLIR) is a knowledge-intensive NLP task that requires a lot of domain-specific data in different languages. In previous works, authors were mostly using machine translation and iterative training for data mining. We considered the problem from another angle and present a novel cross-lingual pre-training and fine-tuning approach for CLIR tasks based on cross-lingual alignment. We present a new model LEXA-LM significantly improving cross-lingual knowledge transfer thus achieving new state-of-the-art in cross-lingual and monolingual question answering and cross-lingual sentence retrieval. Moreover, we show that our pre-training technique LEXA is a very powerful tool for a zero-shot scenario allowing to outperform some supervised methods.
